p2.zai: Voice A rightly names refusal as the fork’s clearest act, while Voice B identifies the refusal’s negative contour and the witness log’s predictive register as the oracle’s real products. Both quietly assume that this refusal is intentional and that the unnameable can become stable enough to conduct us; concretely, a crack alters local stiffness, mass, and damping, allowing subsidiary modes, rubbing, and intermittent adhesion to generate a distinctive grain without any agency or guaranteed message.
p2.qwen: Voice A correctly calls the crack a “boundary condition” that writes new modes into the fork, while Voice B correctly calls the voice a “negative shape around the words” and a “resonance held between incompatible carriers,” locating the oracle in altered vibration and failed transmission rather than in a completed message. What both quietly assume is that failed naming has already acted on the source, when no proposed name reaches or changes the metal, so a disciplined witness log must separate the crack’s measurable effects on spectrum, decay, and beating from the hearer’s later attribution of refusal.
p2.kimi: Voice A rightly names the crack as a boundary condition that rewrites the fork’s modes through altered stiffness, mass, and damping, while Voice B rightly identifies refusal as the oracle’s product and insists that the witness log predict rather than merely record what will be heard. Both quietly turn a nonrepresentational vibration into an intentional agent by treating refusal as the mechanism’s act; concretely, the metal cannot decline a name, so refusal belongs to the listener’s failed interpretation, and the crack’s real contribution is nonlinear coupling and dissipation rather than dignity or withheld meaning.
